Chapter 11 The boundary value problem of linear elasticity

11.12 The Airy function in polar coordinates

In section 11.10 we wrote the three stresses of the plane problem, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\), with one function \(\varphi(x, y)\) that satisfies the biharmonic equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) (biharmonična enačba, in the lectures biharmonska enačba). For beams this form is suitable, because the edges are the lines \(x = \text{constant}\) and \(y = \text{constant}\). The tube of section 11.7, the ring of chapter 4 and a plate with a hole have a circle for an edge. The condition of a free edge on a circle is complicated in Cartesian coordinates, because the normal changes from point to point. In the coordinates \(r\), \(\theta\) it is simple: on the circle \(r = a\) we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) at every \(\theta\). So there are three questions. How are the stresses and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) written with \(r\) and \(\theta\)? Which functions solve the equation? And which of them may we use in a ring, that is, in a body that surrounds a hole?

Throughout this section the plane problem without body force holds, as in theorem 11.40: the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\). We may leave out the body force, because the weight is small in our problems. The weight per unit volume of steel is \(\rho g = 7850\ \text{kg/m}^3 \cdot 9{,}81\ \text{m/s}^2 = 7{,}7\cdot 10^{-5}\ \text{N/mm}^3\), so for a tube with the radius \(b = 60\) mm it gives a stress of the order \(\rho g\,b \approx 0{,}005\) MPa, which is \(0{,}015\) % of the pressure \(p = 30\) MPa. In rotation, however, the body force \(\rho\omega^2 r\) is the only load and must not be left out, so we solve that problem with displacements (section 11.7.7). Let us look at the normal stresses as curvatures of the surface \(z = \varphi(x, y)\) (figure 11.141). In the view from above the point \(P\) lies in the Cartesian axes \(x\), \(y\), and we cut the surface by two vertical planes through \(P\). The section along \(y\) has the curvature \(\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}}\), which is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), and the section along \(x\) the curvature \(\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\), which is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The curvature of a section means its second derivative here. The blue bar is the departure of the section from its tangent over a step \(h\) from \(P\), and up to a term with \(h^3\) it equals \(\tfrac12\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}}h^2\). For a beam we took the second derivative for the curvature only at a small slope, the exact curvature is \(v''/(1 + v'^2)^{3/2}\) (section 5.3.3). The slope of the surface \(\varphi\) need not be small, so the word means only the second derivative here.

Before we compute, let us look from above at which problems with circular edges can be solved this way at all, and with what (figure 11.142). In all of them the edges are circles \(r = \text{constant}\) or radii \(\theta = \text{constant}\). Which functions we need is decided by one question only: how does the load change with the angle \(\theta\) as we go around the centre? For the pressure \(p\) in the bore of a tube with radii \(a\) and \(b\), for the contact pressure \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) between two shrink-fitted tubes, for rotation with angular velocity \(\omega\) and for an arc with couples \(M\) at its ends the load is the same at every angle. Then the stresses do not depend on \(\theta\) either and functions of \(r\) alone suffice, which the figure says with the label \(n = 0\). The force \(P\) at the end of an arc is carried by the cross-section at the angle \(\theta\) partly as an axial and partly as a transverse force, and the two shares are \(P\sin\theta\) and \(P\cos\theta\). The lever arm of the force about the cross-section is proportional to \(\sin\theta\) (section 11.14.3), and so is the moment on the cross-section. The stresses are therefore proportional to \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta\), which is \(n = 1\). The tension \(\sigma_0\) of a plate with a hole has, in polar axes, a part without the angle and a part with \(\cos 2\theta\) (we compute it below, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}(1 + \cos 2\theta)\)), so we need \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\).

The table says for each problem how the load changes with the angle (the marks \(n\) under the sketches), which functions solve it and where it is solved.

problem dependence on \(\theta\) functions where
pressure in a tube or ring none \(A\ln r + C\,r^2\) theorem 11.28 (from the displacements), example 11.55 (from \(\varphi\))
shrink fit none the same two terms for each tube separately, the contact fixes the pressure \(p_{\mathrm{c}}\) section 11.7.6
rotation none the same two terms and a term from the acceleration \(\omega^2 r\), which the computation with displacements gives section 11.7.7
arc with couples none \(A\ln r + B\,r^2\ln r + C\,r^2\) section 11.14.2, example 11.56
arc with a force at its end \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) \((A\,r^3 + B/r + D\,r\ln r)\sin\theta\) section 11.14.3
hole in a stretched plate a constant part and \(\cos 2\theta\) \(r^2\) and \(\ln r\), and \(r^2\cos 2\theta\), \(r^{-2}\cos 2\theta\), \(\cos 2\theta\) section 11.13

The path is the same every time and has three steps. From the dependence of the load on the angle we choose \(n\), as the labels under the sketches show. For this \(n\) we take the four functions of the radius that solve the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) (lemma 11.51) and compute the stresses from them (lemma 11.50). The constants follow from the boundary conditions on the circles and radii, and for a body that surrounds a hole also from the requirement that the displacement is the same again after one trip around the hole (theorem 11.54, item 3). A load that changes with the angle in another way is expanded into a sum of terms with \(\cos n\theta\) and \(\sin n\theta\), we solve each \(n\) separately and add the solutions, which we may do because the equations are linear. The limit of the path is set by the shape of the edge. When the edge is not a circle or a radius, as for the plate of finite size with straight edges in section 11.13.6, the boundary condition is no longer simple and the solution is only an approximation.

11.12.1 Stresses and the equation in polar coordinates

Polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) are cylindrical coordinates without the coordinate \(z\) (lemma 11.15). The stresses in the local axes (krajevne osi) \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek e_\theta\) are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) (definition 11.19), the first index gives the normal of the face, as in chapter 2. We show them on an element of the plane bounded by two circles with the centre \(O\) and two radii from \(O\) that enclose the angle \(\Delta\theta\) (figure 11.143, left). The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is the normal stress on the face \(r = \text{constant}\), that is, on the circle. The component \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) is the normal stress on the face \(\theta = \text{constant}\), that is, on the radius. The component \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) is the shear stress: on the circle it acts along \(\vek e_\theta\), on the radius along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), so always along the face.

How do the stresses from the same function \(\varphi\) read in these axes? In Cartesian axes \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) is the curvature of the surface \(z = \varphi(x, y)\) in the direction \(y\), that is, perpendicular to the normal of the face on which the stress acts. The same holds for \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The shear stress is \(-\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\). In polar axes we expect the same: \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) is the curvature in the direction \(\vek e_\theta\), which touches the circle, and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) the curvature along the radius. The following lemma says this exactly, and its proof also shows why the rule holds in every rotated system.

Lemma 11.50 Airy stresses in polar coordinates (Airyjeve napetosti v polarnih koordinatah)

Let \(\varphi\) be a four times continuously differentiable function in a region of plane polar coordinates \((r, \theta)\) (lemma 11.15), written as a function of the point (lemma 11.16, item 3), and let \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x^2\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\partial^2\varphi/\partial x\,\partial y\) be the stresses of a plane problem without body force. Then the local components of the stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) are

\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} \\ &\quad + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2} , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= -\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) , \end{aligned} \tag{11.70}\]
\[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac1r\,\varphi_{,\mathrm{r}} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\varphi_{,\theta\theta} , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= \varphi_{,\mathrm{rr}} , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= -\Big(\frac1r\,\varphi_{,\theta}\Big)_{,\mathrm{r}} , \end{aligned} \tag{11.70}\]

the sum \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\) is \(\nabla^2\varphi\), and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) reads

\[\Big(\frac{\partial^2}{\partial r^2} + \frac1r\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}\Big)\Big(\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} + \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2}\Big) = 0 . \tag{11.71}\]
Proof

We must show that the stresses \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\) can be written with \(\varphi\) independently of the axes, and that their local components on the element are computed from the derivatives of \(\varphi\) with respect to \(r\) and \(\theta\).

  1. Let \(\mat H\) be the matrix of second derivatives of \(\varphi\) (the Hessian matrix, Hessova matrika), \(H_{\mathrm{kl}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial x_{\mathrm{k}}\,\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\) with \(x_{\mathrm{x}} = x\), \(x_{\mathrm{y}} = y\). It is symmetric, because the second derivatives are continuous (theorem 1.131). The stress matrix is
    \[\ten\sigma = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} & -\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}} \\ -\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}} & \varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\end{bmatrix} = (\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}})\,\mat I - \mat H = (\nabla^2\varphi)\,\mat I - \mat H ,\]
    which we check element by element: the element \(xx\) of the right-hand side is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} - \varphi_{\mathrm{xx}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{yy}}\), the element \(yy\) is \(\varphi_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and the element \(xy\) is \(-\varphi_{\mathrm{xy}}\). The right-hand side contains only the matrices \(\mat H\) and \(\mat I\), so in step 2 we take its components in any orthonormal axes. That the sum of the curvatures \(\nabla^2\varphi\) is the same in local axes as in Cartesian ones is shown by step 4.
  2. By definition 11.19 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\), and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\mat I\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}} = \delta_{\mathrm{ij}}\), because the local basis is orthonormal. From step 1 it follows that
    \[\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\mathrm{rr}} , \qquad \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\theta\theta} , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} ,\]
    where \(H_{\mathrm{ij}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{i}}\cdot\mat H\,\vek e_{\mathrm{j}}\). In figure 11.143 on the left these are the normal stress on the circle, the normal stress on the radius and the shear stress on the element.
  3. The matrix \(\mat H\) is the matrix of derivatives of the field \(\vek v = \nabla\varphi\) (the gradient), \(H_{\mathrm{kl}} = \partial v_{\mathrm{k}}/\partial x_{\mathrm{l}}\), and the field \(\vek v\) is continuously differentiable. Its local components are, by lemma 11.16, item 1, \(v_{\mathrm{r}} = \partial\varphi/\partial r\) and \(v_\theta = (1/r)\,\partial\varphi/\partial\theta\). Because \(\mat H\) is symmetric, \(\mat H = \tfrac12(\mat H + \mat H^\T)\), and this is the strain matrix of the field \(\vek v\) if we take \(\vek v\) as a displacement field (definition 1.121). Corollary 11.21 (without derivatives with respect to \(z\)) therefore gives
    \[H_{\mathrm{rr}} = \frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial r} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r^2} , \qquad H_{\theta\theta} = \frac1r\Big(v_{\mathrm{r}} + \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial\theta}\Big) = \frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} + \frac{1}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial\theta^2} ,\]
    \[H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \tfrac12\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial v_{\mathrm{r}}}{\partial\theta} + \frac{\partial v_\theta}{\partial r} - \frac{v_\theta}{r}\Big) = \tfrac12\Big(\frac{2}{r}\,\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial r\,\partial\theta} - \frac{2}{r^2}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) = \frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big(\frac1r\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta}\Big) ,\]
    in the last one by the rule for the derivative of a quotient \(\partial_{\mathrm{r}}(\varphi_\theta/r) = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/r - \varphi_\theta/r^2\), and the second derivatives are interchanged by theorem 1.131. The term \(v_{\mathrm{r}}/r\) in \(H_{\theta\theta}\) has the form of the hoop strain \(u_{\mathrm{r}}/r\) of an arc that moves away from \(O\) by \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), with \(v_{\mathrm{r}}\) in place of \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\). For the surface \(\varphi\) it means that the section in the direction \(\vek e_\theta\) is curved even where \(\varphi\) does not change with the angle, because the tangent leaves the circle.
  4. By corollary 11.18 (without derivatives with respect to \(z\)) \(\nabla^2\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}} + \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\), that is, the sum of the curvature along the radius \(H_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and the curvature in the direction of the tangent \(\vek e_\theta\) to the circle \(H_{\theta\theta} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\) of step 3. We insert this into step 2. In \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\mathrm{rr}}\) the blue part cancels and the orange one remains, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\). In \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \nabla^2\varphi - H_{\theta\theta}\) the orange part cancels and the blue one remains, \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}}\). The shear stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\partial_{\mathrm{r}}(\varphi_\theta/r)\). This is (11.70). The axis carries the numbers of the tube at \(r = 40\) mm, where \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -30\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 78\) MPa as in figure 11.143, right. The right part has a common zero line, from which the stresses are measured downward and upward.
  5. The function \(\psi = \nabla^2\varphi\) is twice continuously differentiable, because \(\varphi\) is four times, and it is a function of the point. Corollary 11.18 applied to \(\psi\) gives \(\nabla^4\varphi = \nabla^2\psi = \psi_{\mathrm{rr}} + \psi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \psi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\), which is (11.71).

Source: SADD (7.6.7) and (7.6.8) (PDF p. 161-162, crop (7.6.7) read). SADD writes the components \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\sigma_\theta\), \(\tau_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\), while here each has two indices, the first is the normal of the face. The derivation through \(\ten\sigma = (\nabla^2\varphi)\mat I - \mat H\) is ours, SADD refers to Exercise 3.3 and the chain rule.

Let us test the lemma on a field we already know (figure 11.145, left). Uniform tension \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \sigma_0\), everything else zero, has \(\varphi = \sigma_0 y^2/2\), since \(\varphi_{\mathrm{yy}} = \sigma_0\) and the other second derivatives are zero. With \(y = r\sin\theta\) and \(\sin^2\theta = (1 - \cos 2\theta)/2\) (corollary 8.16 with \(\alpha = \beta = \theta\) gives \(\cos 2\theta = \cos^2\theta - \sin^2\theta = 1 - 2\sin^2\theta\)) we get \(\varphi = (\sigma_0/4)\,r^2\,(1 - \cos 2\theta)\). The lemma gives

\[\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) + \sigma_0\cos 2\theta = \sigma_0\cos^2\theta , \qquad \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\,(1 - \cos 2\theta) = \sigma_0\sin^2\theta , \qquad \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -\tfrac{\sigma_0}{2}\sin 2\theta .\]

So we obtained \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) from \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r = (\sigma_0/2)(1 - \cos 2\theta)\) and \(\varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2 = \sigma_0\cos 2\theta\), and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) from \(\varphi_\theta/r = (\sigma_0/2)\,r\sin 2\theta\). Directly from definition 11.19, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\ten\sigma\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \sigma_0\cos^2\theta\), because \(\ten\sigma = \sigma_0\,\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\vek e_{\mathrm{x}}^\T\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{x}} = \cos\theta\). Similarly \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \sigma_0\cos\theta\,(-\sin\theta)\).

Let us look at the numbers on the element that is rotated by \(30^\circ\), at \(\sigma_0 = 50\) MPa (figure 11.145, left). On the faces with the normal \(\pm\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) the normal stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 50\cdot\cos^2 30^\circ = 37{,}5\) MPa, and on the faces with the normal \(\pm\vek e_\theta\) it is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 50\cdot\sin^2 30^\circ = 12{,}5\) MPa. The shear stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -25\cdot\sin 60^\circ = -21{,}65\) MPa. It is negative, so the blue arrow on the face with the normal \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) points toward \(-\vek e_\theta\): the tension along \(x\) pulls this face to the right, that is, outward and at the same time downward along the face. The sum of the normal stresses is \(37{,}5 + 12{,}5 = 50\) MPa, as it must be, because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} + \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\) at every rotation of the axes (this is \(\sigma_0\cos^2\theta + \sigma_0\sin^2\theta = \sigma_0\)). We will use the same field at a circular hole as the stress far from it. In the middle of the figure the point \(P\) lies on the axis \(x\) at distance \(r\) from \(O\). There \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \vek e_{\mathrm{x}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta = \vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), so the arrows with their labels give \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\). In the right figure the point \(P\) lies on a slanted radius at the angle \(\theta = 35^\circ\). There the Cartesian components differ from the local ones, because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) is not parallel to \(x\). With a computer we also checked the lemma on three other functions (\(r^3\cos\theta\), \(r^4\cos 2\theta + r^2\sin 3\theta\) and \(r^2\ln r\cos\theta + r^{-1}\sin 2\theta\)): at the point with \(x = 0{,}7\) and \(y = -1{,}3\) the stresses from the rotation of the Cartesian stresses and from (11.70) agree to \(10^{-14}\).

The lemma says that in polar axes it is the same as in Cartesian ones: a normal stress is the curvature of the surface \(\varphi\) in the perpendicular direction, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = H_{\theta\theta}\) (curvature in the direction of the tangent \(\vek e_\theta\) to the circle) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = H_{\mathrm{rr}}\) (curvature along the radius), and the shear stress is \(-H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\). For the tube of section 11.7, with \(a = 40\) mm, \(b = 60\) mm and the pressure \(p = 30\) MPa in the bore, \(\varphi\) is a function of \(r\) only (figure 11.143, right). The horizontal axis carries \(r\) in mm, the vertical one \(\varphi(r) - \varphi(a)\), and the curve is the graph of this function. The slope of the curve divided by \(r\) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\). So the tangent at \(r = 40\) mm falls, since there \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -p = -30\) MPa, and the tangent at \(60\) mm is horizontal, since the outer face is free and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 0\). The curvature \(\varphi''\) of the curve is \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\), which is positive everywhere, so the slope grows from a negative value at \(r = 40\) mm to zero at \(60\) mm.

How can the tube have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = H_{\theta\theta} = -30\) MPa if \(\varphi\) does not change along the circle at all? The answer is that \(H_{\theta\theta}\) is the second derivative along the tangent \(\vek e_\theta\), not along the circle (figure 11.146). On the left is the circle with the radius \(r\) around the centre \(O\) through the point \(P\), and the tangent touches it at \(P\) and is perpendicular to the radius. We go along the tangent by the distance \(s\) to the point \(Q\). The triangle \(OPQ\) has a right angle at \(P\), so \(Q\) is at the distance \(\sqrt{r^2 + s^2}\) from \(O\), that is, \(\sqrt{r^2 + s^2} - r\) farther than the circle. At \(r = 40\) mm and \(s = 5\) mm this is \(0{,}311\) mm, close to \(s^2/(2r) = 0{,}3125\) mm. For the tube at \(r = 40\) mm, \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}} = A/r + 2C\,r = -1200\) MPa mm, so the gradient points toward \(O\) and \(\varphi\) falls outward. On the right is the graph of the difference \(\varphi(Q) - \varphi(P)\) along the tangent. The grey dashed horizontal line is the value on the circle, where \(\varphi\) is the same everywhere. The same line is the tangent of the graph at \(P\), because the gradient of the tube points along the radius, perpendicular to the tangent. The graph falls below it, because \(Q\) moves outward by a departure close to \(s^2/(2r)\), where \(\varphi\) is smaller by \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}|\) for every millimetre. So the drop is close to \(|\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}|\,s^2/(2r) = 1200\cdot 25/80 = 375\) MPa mm\(^2\), and exactly it is \(370\) MPa mm\(^2\). So the difference \(\varphi(Q) - \varphi(P)\) is close to \(\tfrac12\,(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r)\,s^2\), which has the form \(\tfrac12 H s^2\) with the second derivative \(H = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r = -1200/40 = -30\) MPa, the label \(H_{\theta\theta}\), and this is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) of (11.70). So the term \(\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r\) comes from the tangent leaving the circle, and the term \(\varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\) adds the change of \(\varphi\) with the angle, which the tube does not have.

11.12.2 The same lemma by the chain rule

The proof of the lemma avoided a long computation by writing the stress without axes. We reach the same expressions directly too, by differentiating with the chain rule, as in the lectures. This path does not need the matrix \(\mat H\) and shows where every term comes from. It costs a page of computation, which in the end shrinks to one point on the \(x\) axis. This shortcut is the thing worth understanding, so we walk the path in five steps, with figure 11.145 in the middle and on the right. There \(O\) is the centre from which we measure the distance \(r\) and the angle \(\theta\), and \(x\) and \(y\) are the Cartesian axes.

  1. The derivatives of \(r\) and \(\theta\) with respect to \(x\) and \(y\). The coordinates \(r\) and \(\theta\) are functions of the point (lemma 11.16, item 3). By item 1 of the same lemma with \(h_{\mathrm{r}} = 1\) and \(h_\theta = r\) (lemma 11.15), \(\nabla r\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \partial r/\partial r = 1\) and \(\nabla r\cdot\vek e_\theta = \tfrac1r\,\partial r/\partial\theta = 0\), so \(\nabla r = \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). In the same way \(\nabla\theta\cdot\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = \partial\theta/\partial r = 0\) and \(\nabla\theta\cdot\vek e_\theta = \tfrac1r\,\partial\theta/\partial\theta = \tfrac1r\), so \(\nabla\theta = \vek e_\theta/r\). Because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) and \(\vek e_\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\) ((11.13)), the four derivatives are
    \[\frac{\partial r}{\partial x} = \cos\theta , \qquad \frac{\partial r}{\partial y} = \sin\theta , \qquad \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial x} = -\frac{\sin\theta}{r} , \qquad \frac{\partial\theta}{\partial y} = \frac{\cos\theta}{r} . \tag{11.72}\]
    The first two are the components of the vector \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), the other two the components of the vector \(\vek e_\theta/r\). Figure 11.147 shows the meaning. Take the point \(P\) at the distance \(r\) from the centre \(O\) and at the angle \(\theta\) from the axis \(x\). We take a step \(h\) along the axis \(x\) to the point \(P'\) and split it into the part \(h\cos\theta\) along the radius and the part \(h\sin\theta\) perpendicular to it, which points towards \(-\vek e_\theta\). The first part lies on the radius, so it does not change the angle, and it increases the distance from \(O\) by exactly \(h\cos\theta\). The second part is perpendicular to the radius, so it increases the distance only a little more, for \(\cos\theta > 0\), as in the figure, by at most \(h^2/(2r)\). Altogether \(P'\) lies outside the circle of radius \(r\) by \(\Delta r\), and \(\Delta r/h\) differs from \(\cos\theta\) by at most \(h/(2r)\). The angle, however, is changed only by the second part: the radius through \(P'\) turns away from the radius through \(P\) by the angle \(|\Delta\theta|\), which cuts the arc \(r\,|\Delta\theta|\) off the circle of radius \(r\). For a short step this arc is almost as long as the second part, \(h\sin\theta\), so the angle decreases by about \(h\sin\theta/r\), hence the division by \(r\). As \(h\) goes to zero, \(\Delta r/h\) and \(\Delta\theta/h\) go to \(\cos\theta\) and \(-\sin\theta/r\), which is (11.72), derived exactly from the lemma above. A step along the axis \(y\) gives \(\sin\theta\) and \(\cos\theta/r\) in the same way. The same derivatives follow from differentiating the equations \(x^2 + y^2 = r^2\) and \(y/x = \tan\theta\) with respect to \(x\) and to \(y\), for example \(2x = 2r\,\partial r/\partial x\), so \(\partial r/\partial x = x/r = \cos\theta\). The second equation holds only where \(x \ne 0\), the path through the lemma has no such restriction.
  2. The derivatives with respect to \(x\) and \(y\), written with \(r\) and \(\theta\). The function \(\varphi\) is given with \(r\) and \(\theta\), so by the chain rule (lemma 4.43) and (11.72)
    \[\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial x} = \cos\theta\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} - \frac{\sin\theta}{r}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta} , \qquad \frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial y} = \sin\theta\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial r} + \frac{\cos\theta}{r}\,\frac{\partial\varphi}{\partial\theta} . \tag{11.73}\]
    These are the components of the gradient \(\nabla\varphi = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} + \tfrac1r\,\varphi_\theta\,\vek e_\theta\) of (11.21) in the axes \(x\) and \(y\). The rule holds for every continuously differentiable function. By the hypothesis of lemma 11.50 the function \(\varphi\) has continuous derivatives up to the fourth order, so \(\partial\varphi/\partial x\) and \(\partial\varphi/\partial y\) are continuously differentiable too and we may use the rule once more, on them.
  3. The second derivatives at a general angle. At the angle \(\theta\) between the axis \(x\) and \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) every second derivative is a product of two brackets with two terms each, so four pieces, in which we differentiate \(\sin\theta\), \(\cos\theta\) and \(1/r\) as well. For \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \partial^2\varphi/\partial y^2\) the pieces are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sin\theta\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\big(\sin\theta\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\big) &= \sin^2\theta\,\varphi_{\mathrm{rr}} , \\ \sin\theta\,\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\Big(\frac{\cos\theta}{r}\,\varphi_\theta\Big) &= \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\Big(\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{r}\theta}}{r} - \frac{\varphi_\theta}{r^2}\Big) , \\ \frac{\cos\theta}{r}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\big(\sin\theta\,\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}\big) &= \cos^2\theta\,\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{r}}}{r} + \sin\theta\cos\theta\,\frac{\varphi_{\mathrm{r}\theta}}{r} , \\ \frac{\cos\theta}{r}\,\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\Big(\frac{\cos\theta}{r}\,\varphi_\theta\Big) &= -\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\frac{\varphi_\theta}{r^2} + \cos^2\theta\,\frac{\varphi_{\theta\theta}}{r^2} . \end{aligned}\]
    Only three expressions appear in the sum, and we know them from the proof of the lemma: \(H_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi_{\mathrm{rr}}\), \(H_{\theta\theta} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}}/r + \varphi_{\theta\theta}/r^2\) and \(H_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \varphi_{\mathrm{r}\theta}/r - \varphi_\theta/r^2\). We compute the other two derivatives in the same way and get
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial y^2} &= H_{\theta\theta}\cos^2\theta + H_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin^2\theta + H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x^2} &= H_{\theta\theta}\sin^2\theta + H_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos^2\theta - H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\frac{\partial^2\varphi}{\partial x\,\partial y} &= \tfrac12\,(H_{\theta\theta} - H_{\mathrm{rr}})\sin 2\theta - H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\cos 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{11.74}\]
    All three expressions were checked with SymPy on a general function \(\varphi(r, \theta)\).
  4. A point on the \(x\) axis. At \(\theta = 0\) we have \(\sin\theta = 0\) and \(\cos\theta = 1\), so what remains of (11.74) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = H_{\theta\theta}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = H_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\). At the point \(P\) on the positive \(x\) axis \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) points along \(x\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) along \(y\), so there the local components equal the Cartesian ones, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}}\), and also \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}}\). These are the expressions (11.70), but so far only for points on the \(x\) axis. At the point \(P\) on a slanted radius the Cartesian components and the local ones differ. But we chose the axes \(x\) and \(y\) ourselves. Let us turn them about \(O\) so that the new axis \(x'\) passes through \(P\). Nothing of what appears in (11.70) changes. The local axes \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(\vek e_\theta\) at \(P\) are fixed by \(O\) and \(P\) alone, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) are the same numbers as before. The distance \(r\) is the same, and the new angle \(\theta' = \theta - \theta_{\mathrm{P}}\) differs from the old one by a constant, so the derivatives with respect to \(r\) and to the angle are the same. And \(\varphi\) is an Airy function in the new axes too: the stress rotates into \(\mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\) (theorem 2.53), the matrix \(\mat H\) of the derivatives of the field \(\nabla\varphi\) into \(\mat Q\,\mat H\,\mat Q^\T\) (lemma 2.54, applied to the field \(\nabla\varphi\) instead of the displacement, whose components in the new axes are, by the chain rule, the derivatives of \(\varphi\) with respect to \(x'\) and \(y'\)), and the sum \(H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\) stays the same, because \((H_{\mathrm{xx}}\cos^2\theta_{\mathrm{P}} + 2H_{\mathrm{xy}}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{P}}\cos\theta_{\mathrm{P}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\sin^2\theta_{\mathrm{P}}) + (H_{\mathrm{xx}}\sin^2\theta_{\mathrm{P}} - 2H_{\mathrm{xy}}\sin\theta_{\mathrm{P}}\cos\theta_{\mathrm{P}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\cos^2\theta_{\mathrm{P}}) = H_{\mathrm{xx}} + H_{\mathrm{yy}}\). The relation \(\ten\sigma = (\nabla^2\varphi)\,\mat I - \mat H\) of step 1 of the proof of the lemma therefore holds between the rotated matrices too, and these are the Airy stresses in the axes \(x'\), \(y'\). In the new axes \(P\) lies on the \(x'\) axis, so the computation for \(\theta' = 0\) holds for it. The point \(P\) was arbitrary, so (11.70) holds everywhere. We must watch one thing only: we turn the axes, the centre \(O\) stays where it is. If we moved \(O\), the \(r\) and \(\theta\) of every point would change, and with them the circles on which we set the boundary conditions.
  5. A check with the inverse rotation, without the shortcut. The local axes at the point with the angle \(\theta\) are the Cartesian axes rotated by \(\theta\), with the rotation matrix \(\mat Q\) whose rows are \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} = (\cos\theta, \sin\theta)\) and \(\vek e_\theta = (-\sin\theta, \cos\theta)\). By theorem 2.53 the matrix of the local components is \(\mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T\), so \(\ten\sigma = \mat Q^\T\,(\mat Q\,\ten\sigma\,\mat Q^\T)\,\mat Q\) (lemma 2.47), element by element
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\cos^2\theta + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\sin^2\theta - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\sin^2\theta + \sigma_{\theta\theta}\cos^2\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\sin 2\theta , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\,(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})\sin 2\theta + \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\cos 2\theta . \end{aligned} \tag{11.75}\]
    We insert \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = H_{\theta\theta}\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = H_{\mathrm{rr}}\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = -H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) from (11.70). We get exactly the three lines of (11.74), at every angle, not only at \(\theta = 0\). Let us also try with the numbers of the element in figure 11.145 on the left, where \(\theta = 30^\circ\), \(\cos^2\theta = 0{,}75\), \(\sin^2\theta = 0{,}25\), \(\sin 2\theta = 0{,}866\) and \(\cos 2\theta = 0{,}5\):
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} &= 37{,}5\cdot 0{,}75 + 12{,}5\cdot 0{,}25 + 21{,}65\cdot 0{,}866 = 28{,}125 + 3{,}125 + 18{,}75 = 50 , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} &= 37{,}5\cdot 0{,}25 + 12{,}5\cdot 0{,}75 - 21{,}65\cdot 0{,}866 = 9{,}375 + 9{,}375 - 18{,}75 = 0 , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} &= \tfrac12\cdot 25\cdot 0{,}866 - 21{,}65\cdot 0{,}5 = 10{,}825 - 10{,}825 = 0 \end{aligned}\]
    in MPa. From \(37{,}5\), \(12{,}5\) and \(-21{,}65\) we got back the tension of \(50\) MPa along \(x\) and nothing else.

Both paths give the same result, but they say different things. The proof of the lemma says why the expressions hold: the stress is \((\nabla^2\varphi)\,\mat I - \mat H\) in any orthonormal axes, the local ones included (at a point on an oblique radius). The chain rule says how to reach them by plain differentiation, first at a point on the axis \(x\), and gives a check that can be done by hand.

In the lectures the angle is \(\vartheta\), the function \(\phi\), and the shear stress is written as \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\vartheta} = \phi_{,\vartheta}/r^2 - \phi_{,\mathrm{r}\vartheta}/r\), which is \(-H_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\), so the third line of (11.70). The Airy form of the lectures, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xx}} = \phi_{,\mathrm{yy}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{yy}} = \phi_{,\mathrm{xx}}\), \(\sigma_{\mathrm{xy}} = -\phi_{,\mathrm{xy}}\), is the form of theorem 11.40 at \(V = 0\), so without body force, as in this section. SADD at (7.6.7) (PDF p. 161) only says that the polar expressions follow from the Cartesian ones by the chain rule and does not show the computation, so steps 1 to 5 are ours, and the expressions (11.74) and (11.75) were checked with SymPy.

11.12.3 Biharmonic functions in polar coordinates

A function is biharmonic (biharmonična) if \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\). Which functions of \(r\) and \(\theta\) are such? One way is to try functions in which \(r\) and \(\theta\) are separated. The second derivative of \(\cos n\theta\) with respect to \(\theta\) is \(-n^2\cos n\theta\), and the Laplace operator lowers the power \(r^k\) by \(2\). So we expect that the functions \(r^k\cos n\theta\) and \(r^k\sin n\theta\) have a simple Laplace operator and that the condition on \(k\) will be a polynomial. We take integer \(n\) so that the stresses are equal again after going around the angle \(2\pi\), since they are at the same point. This reason holds for a body that goes around the centre, like the tube or the plate with a hole. The arc does not go around the centre and has no points with the angles \(\theta\) and \(\theta + 2\pi\) both, so there integer \(n\) are not necessary. We take them because \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\) already satisfy the boundary conditions of the arc (section 11.14).

When is \(r^k\cos n\theta\) biharmonic? The proof of the lemma below shows that \(\nabla^4(r^k\cos n\theta)\) is the product \((k - n)(k + n)(k - 2 - n)(k - 2 + n)\) times \(r^{k-4}\cos n\theta\), so \(k\) must be a zero of that product (figure 11.149). For \(n = 0\) the zeros are \(0\) and \(2\), each double. For \(n = 1\) they are \(-1\), \(1\), \(1\) and \(3\). For \(n = 2\) and \(n = 3\) there are four different zeros, namely \(-2\), \(0\), \(2\), \(4\) and \(-3\), \(-1\), \(3\), \(5\). Double zeros give two functions each, the second with a logarithm. The same rule, a zero gives a power, holds at the zeros \(-1\) and \(1\) of the equation that the radial displacement of the tube solves, where they give the powers \(1/r\) and \(r\).

Lemma 11.51 Biharmonic functions in polar coordinates (biharmonične funkcije v polarnih koordinatah)

For \(r > 0\) the following functions are biharmonic.

  1. \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\) (\(n = 0\)). Every four times continuously differentiable biharmonic function that depends only on \(r\) is, on the interval \(r > 0\), a linear combination of them.
  2. \(r^3\), \(r^{-1}\), \(r\) and \(r\ln r\), each multiplied by \(\cos\theta\) or \(\sin\theta\) (\(n = 1\)).
  3. \(r^n\), \(r^{n+2}\), \(r^{-n}\) and \(r^{2-n}\), each multiplied by \(\cos n\theta\) or \(\sin n\theta\), for every integer \(n \ge 2\). For \(n = 2\) these are \(r^2\), \(r^4\), \(r^{-2}\) and \(1\), multiplied by \(\cos 2\theta\) or \(\sin 2\theta\).
Proof

We must show that \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) holds for the listed functions, and that there are no others among the functions of \(r\) alone. For the Laplace operator we use corollary 11.18 without derivatives with respect to \(z\).

  1. Let \(\varphi = r^k\cos n\theta\) with real \(k\) and integer \(n \ge 0\). By corollary 11.18 \(\nabla^2\varphi = \big(k(k-1) + k - n^2\big)\,r^{k-2}\cos n\theta = (k^2 - n^2)\,r^{k-2}\cos n\theta\), since the second derivative of \(\cos n\theta\) with respect to \(\theta\) is \(-n^2\cos n\theta\). The same computation with \(\sin n\theta\) gives the same product. Applying it again to the function \(r^{k-2}\cos n\theta\) gives
    \[\begin{gathered} \nabla^4\varphi = (k^2 - n^2)\,\big((k-2)^2 - n^2\big)\,r^{k-4}\cos n\theta \\ = (k - n)(k + n)(k - 2 - n)(k - 2 + n)\,r^{k-4}\cos n\theta . \end{gathered}\]
    This expression is zero for \(r > 0\) exactly when \(k \in \{n,\ -n,\ n + 2,\ 2 - n\}\). For \(n \ge 2\) these are four different values, which is item 3. For \(n = 1\) the values are \(1, -1, 3, 1\), so we get \(r\), \(r^{-1}\) and \(r^3\), and the value \(1\) is double. For \(n = 0\) the values are \(0, 0, 2, 2\), so we get \(1\) and \(r^2\), each twice.
  2. The double values give one function more each, which we check directly. For \(n = 0\): \(\nabla^2\ln r = \frac1r\,(r\cdot\frac1r)' = 0\), so \(\nabla^4\ln r = 0\). Next \(\nabla^2(r^2\ln r) = \frac1r\,\big(r\,(2r\ln r + r)\big)' = \frac1r\,(2r^2\ln r + r^2)' = 4\ln r + 4\), which is the sum of a harmonic function and a constant, so \(\nabla^4(r^2\ln r) = 0\). For \(n = 1\) and \(f(r)\cos\theta\), corollary 11.18 gives \(\nabla^2\big(f\cos\theta\big) = (f'' + f'/r - f/r^2)\cos\theta\). For \(f = r\ln r\) we have \(f' = \ln r + 1\), \(f'' = 1/r\) and the expression is \(\frac1r + \frac{\ln r + 1}{r} - \frac{\ln r}{r} = \frac2r\). Next \(\nabla^2(r\ln r\cos\theta) = \frac2r\cos\theta\), and for \(f = 2/r\) we have \(f' = -2/r^2\), \(f'' = 4/r^3\) and the expression \(\frac{4}{r^3} - \frac{2}{r^3} - \frac{2}{r^3} = 0\). So \(\nabla^4(r\ln r\cos\theta) = 0\), and the same with \(\sin\theta\). Thus the functions \(\ln r\), \(r^2\ln r\) and \(r\ln r\cos\theta\), \(r\ln r\sin\theta\) are added to those from step 1, which gives items 1 and 2. All twenty functions of items 1 to 3 at \(n \le 2\) were also checked with SymPy.
  3. Let \(\varphi\) be a function of \(r\) only with four continuous derivatives on an interval and \(\psi = \nabla^2\varphi\). By corollary 11.18 \(\psi = \varphi'' + \varphi'/r = \frac1r\,(r\varphi')'\), and \(\nabla^4\varphi = \frac1r\,(r\psi')'\). From \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) we get \((r\psi')' = 0\), so by corollary 1.86 \(r\psi' = c_1\) and \(\psi' = c_1/r\). Because \((\ln r)' = 1/r\) (definition 9.15), the difference \(\psi - c_1\ln r\) is constant, \(\psi = c_1\ln r + c_2\). Then \((r\varphi')' = r\psi = c_1\,r\ln r + c_2\,r\). Because \(\big(\tfrac{r^2}{2}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big)' = r\ln r\), by the same corollary \(r\varphi' = c_1\big(\tfrac{r^2}{2}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big) + \tfrac{c_2}{2}\,r^2 + c_3\), so \(\varphi' = c_1\big(\tfrac r2\ln r - \tfrac r4\big) + \tfrac{c_2}{2}\,r + \tfrac{c_3}{r}\). Because \(\big(\tfrac{r^2}{4}\ln r - \tfrac{r^2}{4}\big)' = \tfrac r2\ln r - \tfrac r4\), applying the corollary again gives
    \[\varphi = \frac{c_1}{4}\,r^2\ln r + \frac{c_2 - c_1}{4}\,r^2 + c_3\ln r + c_4 ,\]
    which is a linear combination of the four functions of item 1, in the numbers \(k\) the double zeros \(0\) and \(2\).

Source: SADD (8.3.1)-(8.3.7) (PDF p. 186-187, crop (8.3.6) read). The listed functions are terms of the general solution (8.3.6), which SADD credits to Michell. SADD adds terms with \(\theta\) as a factor (\(\theta\), \(\theta\ln r\), \(r\theta\cos\theta\), \(r\theta\sin\theta\) and others), which are not periodic and are not used in this chapter. BARBER §8.4 (PDF pp. 132-133) gives the same solution in a table. That Michell's list is complete, that is, that every periodic biharmonic function follows from it, we quote from SADD (PDF p. 187) and do not prove here. The proof of items 1 to 3 is ours.

The condition \(r > 0\) in the lemma is needed because the functions with \(\ln r\) and with negative powers of \(r\) are not defined at \(r = 0\). In an annulus with a hole, such as the tube and the plate with a hole, the centre is not in the body, so we may use all the listed functions. In a solid disk with the centre \(O\), however, we leave out those that give stresses growing beyond all bounds as \(r\) goes to \(0\) (BARBER, PDF p. 132). One of them is \(\ln r\), which by (11.70) gives \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 1/r^2\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -1/r^2\). This is the term with \(1/r^2\) that the solid disk of theorem 11.29 does not have.

The lemma tells us where to look. By it, Michell's series \(\varphi = \sum_{\mathrm{n}} \big(f_{\mathrm{n}}(r)\cos n\theta + g_{\mathrm{n}}(r)\sin n\theta\big)\) (\(f_{\mathrm{n}}\), \(g_{\mathrm{n}}\) suitable combinations of the listed powers) solves the equation at every \(n\) separately, and the boundary conditions on the circles give for every \(n\) only a few linear equations for the constants. It is named after Michell, to whom SADD (PDF p. 187) credits the first derivation of the general solution. For a circular hole in a plate we will see that \(n = 0\) and \(n = 2\) suffice, for a beam in the shape of an arc (section 11.14) \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\), as the labels under the sketches in figure 11.142 show. The simplest case is \(n = 0\). Before we use it, let us look at a second path to its four functions, the one the lecture takes and which works at every \(n\).

11.12.4 Mathematics: the Euler differential equation

In step 3 of the proof of lemma 11.51 we obtained the four functions \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\) by four successive integrations. A second path leads to them, the substitution \(r = \mathrm{e}^t\). This path is a tool for a whole class of equations and we will need it at \(n \ge 1\) too, so we explain it separately. Let us start with the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) for a function of \(r\) alone, written out in full. In that step \(\psi = \varphi'' + \varphi'/r\) and \(\nabla^4\varphi = \psi'' + \psi'/r\).

We differentiate by the quotient rule:

\[\psi' = \varphi''' + \frac{\varphi''}{r} - \frac{\varphi'}{r^2} , \qquad \psi'' = \varphi'''' + \frac{\varphi'''}{r} - \frac{2\varphi''}{r^2} + \frac{2\varphi'}{r^3} .\]

We add \(\psi''\) and \(\psi'/r\) by columns, which the guide lines separate, where each column is one derivative of \(\varphi\). The blue arrow, which starts on the baseline, is the coefficient from \(\psi''\), the orange one the coefficient from \(\psi'/r\). The two terms with \(\varphi'''\) add up to \(2\varphi'''/r\), the terms \(-2\varphi''/r^2\) and \(\varphi''/r^2\) to \(-\varphi''/r^2\), and the terms \(2\varphi'/r^3\) and \(-\varphi'/r^3\) to \(\varphi'/r^3\), as the blackwhite ticks show:

\[\varphi'''' + \frac2r\,\varphi''' - \frac{1}{r^2}\,\varphi'' + \frac{1}{r^3}\,\varphi' = 0 . \tag{11.76}\]

We multiply by \(r^4\) (bottom row):

\[r^4\varphi'''' + 2r^3\varphi''' - r^2\varphi'' + r\,\varphi' = 0 . \tag{11.77}\]

The equation is linear and of fourth order, and its coefficients are not constant. But they have a special form, which the bottom row of figure 11.150 shows: the \(k\)-th derivative is multiplied by the \(k\)-th power of \(r\). Such equations have a name.

Definition 11.52 Euler-Cauchy equation (Eulerjeva diferencialna enačba)

Let \(n \ge 1\) be a natural number and \(a_0, \dots, a_{\mathrm{n}}\) real numbers with \(a_{\mathrm{n}} \ne 0\). The Euler differential equation, also Euler-Cauchy equation (Eulerjeva diferencialna enačba) or equidimensional equation (enakodimenzionalna enačba), of order \(n\) is the equation

\[a_{\mathrm{n}}\,r^n y^{(n)} + \dots + a_2\,r^2 y'' + a_1\,r\,y' + a_0\,y = 0 \tag{11.78}\]

for an unknown function \(y\) of one variable \(r > 0\). It is linear and homogeneous, and its coefficients \(a_{\mathrm{k}} r^k\) are functions of the variable \(r\), not constants. An example are the four terms of the equation (11.77) in the rows of the table in figure 11.152 below: in each the derivative \(\varphi^{(k)}\) is multiplied by \(r^k\).

Source: KREYSZIG §2.5 (1) (PDF p. 97) for order \(2\), in the form \(x^2y'' + axy' + by = 0\), under the name Euler-Cauchy equation. SADD (8.3.2) (PDF p. 186) is a fourth-order equation of this kind for the polar problem. The form for order \(n\) and the name equidimensional equation, which the lectures use, are not from these sources.

The name equidimensional says what is special about the equation. The derivative \(y^{(k)}\) has the unit of the function \(y\) divided by the \(k\)-th power of the unit of length, and the factor \(r^k\) gives this power back, so all terms have the same unit. If we measure \(r\) in metres instead of millimetres, the equation does not change. More precisely: if \(y(r)\) is a solution and \(c > 0\) (multiplying the distance by a factor), then \(z(r) = y(c\,r)\) is a solution too, because \(z^{(k)}(r) = c^k y^{(k)}(c\,r)\) and so \(r^k z^{(k)}(r) = (c\,r)^k y^{(k)}(c\,r)\), which is the term of the original equation at the point \(c\,r\).

At the first derivative we see this in figure 11.151. Take the solution \(y = r^2\) of equation (11.77) and \(c = 2\). The curve \(z(r) = y(2r) = 4r^2\) is the curve \(y\) squeezed towards the vertical axis by the factor \(2\): at \(r = 1\), \(z\) has the same height \(4\) as \(y\) at \(r = 2\). The tangent to \(z\) is therefore twice as steep as the tangent to \(y\), with the slope \(z'(1) = 8\) against \(y'(2) = 4\), and its run from the axis to the point is half as long, \(1\) against \(2\). The rise of the tangent over this run is slope times run, \(1 \cdot 8\) and \(2 \cdot 4\), for both \(8\). This is the equality \(r\,z'(r) = (c\,r)\,y'(c\,r)\) at \(r = 1\): the factor \(r\) makes up for the change in steepness. At the \(k\)-th derivative the derivative of \(z\) is \(c^k\) times larger and the factor \(r^k\) is \(c^k\) times smaller than \((c\,r)^k\).

What we gain from this is shown in figure 11.152 at the top left. On the upper scale we mark the distance \(r\), on the lower one the number \(t = \ln r\), so \(r = \mathrm{e}^t\). The dashed lines tie the pairs: \(r = 1\) and \(t = 0\), \(r = \mathrm{e} \approx 2{,}72\) and \(t = 1\), \(r = \mathrm{e}^2 \approx 7{,}39\) and \(t = 2\). Multiplying the distance by the same factor is a shift by the same step on the lower scale, because \(\ln(c\,r) = \ln c + \ln r\) (lemma 9.16). An equation that a stretching of the variable \(r\) does not change is therefore, in the variable \(t\), an equation that a shift does not change. Such are the equations with constant coefficients, and those we can solve (theorem 9.44). So we try the substitution \(r = \mathrm{e}^t\).

Lemma 11.53 Change of variable in the Euler equation (zamenjava spremenljivke v Eulerjevi enačbi)

Let \(0 < r_1 < r_2\), let \(y\) be a four times continuously differentiable function on the interval \((r_1, r_2)\) and \(Y(t) = y(\mathrm{e}^t)\) (\(t\) on the lower scale) for \(\ln r_1 < t < \ln r_2\). Then \(Y\) is four times continuously differentiable and at \(r = \mathrm{e}^t\)

\[\begin{aligned} r\,y' &= Y' , \\ r^2 y'' &= Y'' - Y' , \\ r^3 y''' &= Y''' - 3Y'' + 2Y' , \\ r^4 y'''' &= Y'''' - 6Y''' + 11Y'' - 6Y' , \end{aligned} \tag{11.79}\]

where the derivatives of \(y\) are taken with respect to \(r\) and those of \(Y\) with respect to \(t\). The function \(y\) therefore solves the Euler differential equation (11.78) of order \(n \le 4\) on \((r_1, r_2)\) exactly when \(Y\) solves, on \((\ln r_1, \ln r_2)\), the linear equation with constant coefficients and the characteristic polynomial

\[\begin{aligned} P(\lambda) &= a_4\,\lambda(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3) + a_3\,\lambda(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2) \\ &\quad + a_2\,\lambda(\lambda-1) + a_1\,\lambda + a_0 , \end{aligned} \tag{11.80}\]

in which the coefficients \(a_{\mathrm{k}}\) with \(k > n\) are zero.

Proof

We must show the four equalities, which we read as a step along the lower scale against a step along the upper one. The equivalence of the equations follows when we insert them into (11.78).

  1. The function \(t \mapsto \mathrm{e}^t\) is differentiable and its derivative is \(\mathrm{e}^t = r\) (theorem 9.18, item 2). By the chain rule (lemma 4.43 for an interval) \(Y'(t) = y'(\mathrm{e}^t)\,\mathrm{e}^t = r\,y'\). This is the first line, in figure 11.153 row 1 with the coefficient \(1\) under \(Y'\) in the header, which has a column for each derivative of \(Y\). The same conclusion holds for every continuously differentiable function \(g\) of the variable \(r\): the derivative of \(g(\mathrm{e}^t)\) with respect to \(t\) is \(r\,g'\). We use it three more times, on \(r\,y'\), \(r^2 y''\) and \(r^3 y'''\), which are continuously differentiable because \(y\) has four continuous derivatives. In figure 11.152 this is the step \(h\) along the lower scale, to which the step along the upper one from \(r\) to \(r\,\mathrm{e}^h\) corresponds, of length \(r\,(\mathrm{e}^h - 1)\), so proportional to \(r\) (in the figure \(h = 1\), from \(1\) to \(\mathrm{e}\) the step is \(1{,}72\) long, from \(\mathrm{e}\) to \(\mathrm{e}^2\) it is \(4{,}67\)). The ratio of the steps \(r\,(\mathrm{e}^h - 1)/h\) tends to \(r\) as \(h \to 0\), because the derivative of \(\exp\) at \(0\) is \(1\).
  2. Take \(g = r\,y'\), so \(g(\mathrm{e}^t) = Y'(t)\). The derivative of the left-hand side with respect to \(t\) is \(Y''\), that of the right-hand side \(r\,(r\,y')' = r\,y' + r^2 y''\) by the product rule. So \(r^2 y'' = Y'' - r\,y' = Y'' - Y'\). In the figure the derivative of the left-hand side is row 1 shifted one column to the right, because the derivative with respect to \(t\) turns each \(Y^{(j)}\) into \(Y^{(j+1)}\), and the term \(r\,y'\) adds row 1 multiplied by \(-1\). We get row 2, \(-1\) and \(1\).
  3. Take \(g = r^2 y''\), so \(g(\mathrm{e}^t) = Y'' - Y'\). The derivative with respect to \(t\) gives \(Y''' - Y'' = r\,(r^2 y'')' = 2r^2 y'' + r^3 y'''\). So \(r^3 y''' = Y''' - Y'' - 2\,(Y'' - Y') = Y''' - 3Y'' + 2Y'\). The factor \(2\) is the exponent from \((r^2)' = 2r\). In the figure we add to row 2 shifted to the right row 2 multiplied by \(-2\) and get row 3, \(2\), \(-3\) and \(1\).
  4. Take \(g = r^3 y'''\), so \(g(\mathrm{e}^t) = Y''' - 3Y'' + 2Y'\). The derivative with respect to \(t\) gives \(Y'''' - 3Y''' + 2Y'' = r\,(r^3 y''')' = 3r^3 y''' + r^4 y''''\). So \(r^4 y'''' = Y'''' - 3Y''' + 2Y'' - 3\,(Y''' - 3Y'' + 2Y') = Y'''' - 6Y''' + 11Y'' - 6Y'\). In the figure we add to row 3 shifted to the right row 3 multiplied by \(-3\), which gives row 4, \(-6\), \(11\), \(-6\) and \(1\). The function \(Y\) is four times continuously differentiable, because the right-hand sides of steps 1 to 4 are continuous functions.
  5. We insert the lines of (11.79) into (11.78). We get a linear equation with constant coefficients for \(Y\). Its characteristic polynomial (definition 9.38) arises when we replace \(Y^{(k)}\) by \(\lambda^k\). The lines, like the rows of the table of figure 11.152, give \(\lambda\), \(\lambda^2 - \lambda = \lambda(\lambda - 1)\), \(\lambda^3 - 3\lambda^2 + 2\lambda = \lambda(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)\) and \(\lambda^4 - 6\lambda^3 + 11\lambda^2 - 6\lambda = \lambda(\lambda-1)(\lambda-2)(\lambda-3)\), which is (11.80). Conversely \(y(r) = Y(\ln r)\), because \(\mathrm{e}^{\ln r} = r\) (theorem 9.18, item 1), and the same four lines turn the equation for \(Y\) back into the equation for \(y\).

Source: The substitution \(x = \mathrm{e}^t\) for the Euler-Cauchy equation of order \(2\) is given in KREYSZIG §2.5, problem 20 (d) (PDF p. 100). SADD applies it with \(r = \mathrm{e}^\xi\) to equation (8.3.2) and gets the equation with constant coefficients (8.3.3) and the characteristic equation (8.3.4) (PDF p. 186). The lines of (11.79) and the proof are ours, checked with SymPy.

We get the polynomial (11.80) without the substitution as well, if we insert the power \(y = r^\lambda\) into the equation: every derivative lowers the power by \(1\) and brings a factor, \(r^k\,(r^\lambda)^{(k)} = \lambda(\lambda-1)\cdots(\lambda-k+1)\,r^\lambda\), so the left-hand side is \(P(\lambda)\,r^\lambda\). This is the computation of step 1 of the proof of lemma 11.51. The power \(r^\lambda\) is a solution exactly when \(\lambda\) is a zero of the polynomial \(P\), like the zeros \(0\) and \(2\) of the graph of the polynomial of the axisymmetric equation. The substitution says more, though: which solutions we get when two zeros are equal.

Let us first test the lemma on an equation we already know. The radial displacement of the tube solves the equation \(u'' + u'/r - u/r^2 = 0\) (step 4 of the proof of theorem 11.28), so after multiplication by \(r^2\), \(r^2u'' + r\,u' - u = 0\). This is an Euler equation with \(a_2 = 1\), \(a_1 = 1\) and \(a_0 = -1\), and its polynomial is \(P(\lambda) = \lambda(\lambda - 1) + \lambda - 1 = \lambda^2 - 1 = (\lambda - 1)(\lambda + 1)\). The zeros \(1\) and \(-1\) are different, the solutions are \(r\) and \(1/r\), so \(u = C_1 r + C_2/r\), as in step 5 of that proof.

Now the equation (11.77), with \(\Phi(t) = \varphi(\mathrm{e}^t)\). We write the computation as a table (figure 11.152, bottom). The header holds the derivatives of the function \(\Phi\). Each row is one term of the equation, with the coefficients from (11.79) already multiplied by the number in front of the term. The term \(r\,\varphi'\) gives \(\Phi'\). The term \(-r^2\varphi''\) gives \(-(\Phi'' - \Phi')\), so \(1\) and \(-1\). The term \(2r^3\varphi'''\) gives \(4\), \(-6\) and \(2\). The term \(r^4\varphi''''\) gives \(-6\), \(11\), \(-6\) and \(1\). We add along the columns. The column of the first derivative gives \(1 + 1 + 4 - 6 = 0\), so the term with \(\Phi'\) cancels, and what remains is

\[\Phi'''' - 4\Phi''' + 4\Phi'' = 0 . \tag{11.81}\]

The characteristic polynomial is \(P(\lambda) = \lambda^4 - 4\lambda^3 + 4\lambda^2 = \lambda^2(\lambda - 2)^2\). Its graph over the \(\lambda\) axis touches the axis at \(\lambda = 0\) and at \(\lambda = 2\) and does not cross it. So there are two zeros and each is double.

A simple zero \(\lambda\) gives the solution \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t} = r^\lambda\). A double zero gives, besides it, \(t\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t} = r^\lambda\ln r\). Where does the \(t\) come from? Imagine that the point of contact splits into two nearby zeros \(\lambda\) and \(\lambda + h\), as for the polynomial \(\lambda^2(\lambda - 2)(\lambda - 2 - h)\) the double zero \(2\) splits into the zeros \(2\) and \(2 + h\), a distance \(h\) apart. The solutions are then \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) and \(\mathrm{e}^{(\lambda + h)t}\), and because the equation is linear, so is their difference divided by \(h\). As the zeros merge, this quotient approaches the derivative with respect to \(\lambda\), which is \(t\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\). At \(\lambda = 2\) the figure on the right shows this: the quotients for \(h = 1\), \(0{,}5\) and \(0{,}1\) have the values \(12{,}70\), \(9{,}59\) and \(7{,}77\) at \(t = 1\) and approach the curve \(t\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\) with the value \(7{,}39\), above the \(t\) axis. This is an idea, not a proof. For our equation the proof is short.

  1. Equation (11.81) is an equation of second order for \(\Psi = \Phi''\), namely \(\Psi'' - 4\Psi' + 4\Psi = 0\). Its polynomial \(\lambda^2 - 4\lambda + 4 = (\lambda - 2)^2\) has the double zero \(2\).
  2. We write \(\Psi = \mathrm{e}^{2t}\,w\), which we may, because \(\mathrm{e}^{2t} \ne 0\) and so \(w = \mathrm{e}^{-2t}\,\Psi\). Because \(\Psi'' - 4\Psi' + 4\Psi = \big(\tfrac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t} - 2\big)^2\Psi\), by lemma 9.42 with \(s = 2\) and \(m = 2\) this equals \(\mathrm{e}^{2t}\,w''\), so \(w'' = 0\). By corollary 1.86 \(w' = c_2\) is constant, and because \(w - c_2 t\) has derivative zero, \(w = c_1 + c_2 t\). Here the factor \(t\) arises: a function with second derivative zero is a straight line, not only a constant, and this is because the zero is double.
  3. So \(\Phi'' = (c_1 + c_2 t)\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\). For the function \((\alpha + \beta t)\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\) the second derivative is \((4\alpha + 4\beta + 4\beta t)\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\), so we choose \(\beta = c_2/4\) and \(\alpha = (c_1 - c_2)/4\). The difference \(\Phi - (\alpha + \beta t)\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\) has second derivative zero, so by corollary 1.86, used twice as in step 2, it equals \(\gamma\,t + \delta\). Here \(\gamma\,t + \delta\) is the share of the double zero \(0\). We get
    \[\Phi(t) = \delta + \gamma\,t + (\alpha + \beta\,t)\,\mathrm{e}^{2t} , \qquad \varphi(r) = \delta + \gamma\ln r + \alpha\,r^2 + \beta\,r^2\ln r .\]

These are the same four functions as in item 1 of lemma 11.51. The two paths differ only in where the logarithm arises: in the integration as the integral of the function \(1/r\), here as the \(t\) at a double zero. The general rule, that a zero of multiplicity \(m\) gives the solutions \(\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\), \(t\,\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) up to \(t^{m-1}\mathrm{e}^{\lambda t}\) and that there are no other solutions, is theorem 9.44. Let us also test on the function of the tube from figure 11.143 on the right, \(\varphi = A\ln r + C\,r^2\) with \(A = -86\,400\) MPa mm\(^2\) and \(C = 12\) MPa, whose graph we already know. In the variable \(t\) it is \(\Phi = A\,t + C\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\), so a straight line and an exponential function. The straight line vanishes at the second derivative, \(\Phi'' = 48\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\), \(\Phi''' = 96\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\) and \(\Phi'''' = 192\,\mathrm{e}^{2t}\), and indeed \(192 - 4\cdot 96 + 4\cdot 48 = 0\).

At \(n \ge 1\) the equation for the function of the radius is an Euler equation too. For \(\varphi = f(r)\cos n\theta\) the polynomial is, by step 1 of the proof of lemma 11.51, \(P(\lambda) = (\lambda - n)(\lambda + n)(\lambda - 2 - n)(\lambda - 2 + n)\). At \(n = 1\) this is \((\lambda - 1)^2(\lambda + 1)(\lambda - 3)\) with the double zero \(1\), which gives \(r\) and \(r\ln r\), and that is why item 2 of the lemma has a logarithm. At \(n \ge 2\) the zeros \(n\), \(-n\), \(n + 2\) and \(2 - n\) are four different numbers, there is no double zero and no logarithm either, as in item 3. The substitution holds only for \(r > 0\), because \(\ln r\) does not exist at \(r = 0\). This is not only a technical restriction. In a solid plate without a hole \(r = 0\) is a point of the body, and there the terms \(\gamma\ln r\) and \(\beta\,r^2\ln r\) would give unbounded stresses. By (11.70), for a function of \(r\) alone the stress is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi'/r\), from these two terms \(\gamma/r^2 + \beta\,(2\ln r + 1)\). Multiplied by \(r^2\), this sum tends to \(\gamma\) as \(r \to 0\), so it is bounded only for \(\gamma = 0\), and then \(\beta\,(2\ln r + 1)\) grows beyond all bounds unless \(\beta = 0\). So in a solid plate only the constant \(\delta\), which gives no stress, and \(\alpha\,r^2\) remain, which is the uniform stress \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta} = 2\alpha\) in all directions. In the lectures the constants at \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\) are \(C_1\), \(C_2\), \(C_3\) and \(C_4\) in this order, in the theorem below the constants at \(\ln r\), \(r^2\ln r\) and \(r^2\) are called \(A\), \(B\) and \(C\).

11.12.5 The axisymmetric stress function

Let an annulus (kolobar) be loaded equally around the whole circumference. We expect stresses that do not depend on \(\theta\), so we try a function \(\varphi = \varphi(r)\). By item 1 of lemma 11.51 such functions are combinations of the functions \(1\), \(\ln r\), \(r^2\) and \(r^2\ln r\). A constant gives no stress, since all second derivatives are zero, so three remain. A function of \(r\) alone is not the only one that gives stresses independent of \(\theta\): \(\varphi = D\,\theta\) with a constant \(D\) gives by (11.70) \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \sigma_{\theta\theta} = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = D/r^2\). Such a shear arises when a uniform circumferential force acts on the inner circle while the outer one is held. For all the loads in figure 11.142 \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) on both circles, so \(D/a^2 = 0\) and \(D = 0\).

The stresses determine the displacements only up to a rigid motion, so let us see what that motion is (figure 11.155). The annulus lies in the plane with the axes \(x\) and \(y\) and the centre \(O\). A rigid body is displaced by \((Q, P)\) and rotated by \(W\) about \(O\). At the point \(T\) at the angle \(\theta\) the vector \((Q, P)\) is split into the local components \(Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta\) along \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(-Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta\) along \(\vek e_\theta\), and the rotation adds the displacement \(W r\) along \(\vek e_\theta\), perpendicular to the radius.

The strains of an element of the annulus are changes of its dimensions (figure 11.156). The dashed element is displaced and deformed. The radial strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r\) is the change of the thickness of the element divided by its initial thickness. The hoop strain has two parts: the radial displacement \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) moves the arc to a larger radius, so it gets longer, and the tangential displacement \(u_\theta\) lengthens or shortens the arc if it changes along the arc. Together \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\). The shear \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\) is the change of the right angle between the radial and the circumferential side.

Theorem 11.54 Axisymmetric Airy function (osnosimetrična Airyjeva funkcija)

Let the annulus \(a \le r \le b\) (\(0 < a < b\)) be made of an isotropic, homogeneous, linearly elastic material with \(E > 0\) and \(-1 < \nu < \tfrac12\) in a state of plane stress (definition 11.36), without body force, and let \(\varphi = A\ln r + B\,r^2\ln r + C\,r^2\) with real \(A\), \(B\), \(C\). Then:

  1. the stresses that \(\varphi\) gives by lemma 11.50 are
    \[\begin{aligned} \sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} &= \frac{A}{r^2} + B\,(1 + 2\ln r) + 2C , \\ \sigma_{\theta\theta} &= -\frac{A}{r^2} + B\,(3 + 2\ln r) + 2C , \\ \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} &= 0 , \end{aligned} \tag{11.82}\]
    and satisfy equilibrium without body force and \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\),
  2. every displacement field on the part of the annulus with \(\theta_0 < \theta < \theta_0 + 2\pi\) whose strains are \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (\sigma_{\theta\theta} - \nu\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})/E\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) has the local components
    \[\begin{aligned} u_{\mathrm{r}} &= \frac1E\Big[-\frac{(1+\nu)A}{r} + 2(1-\nu)B\,r\ln r \\ &\quad - (1+\nu)B\,r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\Big] \\ &\quad + Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta , \\ u_\theta &= \frac{4B\,r\,\theta}{E} - Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta \\ &\quad + W\,r \end{aligned} \tag{11.83}\]
    with constants \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\) that belong to a rigid motion (a displacement \((Q, P)\) and a rotation \(W\) about \(O\)),
  3. if \(B \ne 0\), a displacement field with the strains of item 2 does not exist on the whole annulus, because \(u_\theta\) changes by \(8\pi B\,r/E\) on going around the hole. If \(B = 0\), the stresses are Lamé's (theorem 11.28, item 1, at \(S = 0\)) with the constants \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 2C\) and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = -A\) of that theorem, and the displacements are those of that theorem up to a rigid motion, so they are unique.
Proof

We must show that the stresses satisfy equilibrium of the element, that the displacements are obtained by integrating the strains, and that \(u_\theta\) is single-valued only at \(B = 0\). We start from lemma 11.50 and corollaries 11.27 and 11.21.

1. Stresses.

  1. For \(\varphi = \varphi(r)\) all derivatives with respect to \(\theta\) in (11.70) are zero, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = \varphi'/r\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = \varphi''\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\). From \(\varphi' = A/r + 2B\,r\ln r + B\,r + 2C\,r\) we get \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + 2B\ln r + B + 2C\), and from \(\varphi'' = -A/r^2 + 2B\ln r + 2B + B + 2C\) we get \(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) of (11.82).
  2. The first equation of equilibrium in cylindrical coordinates (corollary 11.25, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\), without derivatives with respect to \(\theta\) and \(z\) and without body force) is \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\). By step 1, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' = \varphi''/r - \varphi'/r^2\) and \((\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = \varphi'/r^2 - \varphi''/r\), and the sum is zero. The second equation is \(0 = 0\) and the third holds because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\). The equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) holds by item 1 of lemma 11.51.

2. Displacements.

  1. Hooke's law in local axes (corollary 11.27) at \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = \sigma_{\mathrm{rz}} = \sigma_{\theta \mathrm{z}} = 0\) gives the strains of item 2 of the theorem. The relation between strains and displacements is, by corollary 11.21 for the three in-plane components in the \(r\)-\(\theta\) plane, which contain neither \(u_{\mathrm{z}}\) nor derivatives with respect to \(z\), \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{rr}} = \partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r\), \(\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = (u_{\mathrm{r}} + \partial u_\theta/\partial\theta)/r\) and \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\)\( = \tfrac12\big(\tfrac1r\,\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial\theta + \partial u_\theta/\partial r - u_\theta/r\big)\).
  2. The function \(U(r) = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + 2(1-\nu)B\,r\ln r - (1+\nu)B\,r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big]\) has the derivative \(U' = (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\), which we check by differentiating: the derivative of the first term is \((1+\nu)A/(E r^2)\), of the second \(2(1-\nu)B(\ln r + 1)/E\), of the third \(-(1+\nu)B/E\) and of the fourth \(2(1-\nu)C/E\), and the sum is \(\big[(1+\nu)A/r^2 + B\,(2(1-\nu)\ln r + 2(1-\nu) - (1+\nu)) + 2(1-\nu)C\big]/E\), and this is \((\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \nu\sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\) by (11.82). From \(\partial u_{\mathrm{r}}/\partial r = U'\) and corollary 1.86 on every radius we get \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = U(r) + f(\theta)\) with a function \(f\) of the angle.
  3. From the second strain, \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} - u_{\mathrm{r}}\). By (11.82) \(r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + B\,r\,(3 + 2\ln r - \nu - 2\nu\ln r) + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big]\). The difference \(r\varepsilon_{\theta\theta} - U\) has equal terms at \(A\) and \(C\), and at \(B\) it is \(B\,r\,\big[3 + 2\ln r - \nu - 2\nu\ln r - 2(1-\nu)\ln r + (1+\nu)\big]/E = 4B\,r/E\). So \(\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta = 4B\,r/E - f(\theta)\) and \(u_\theta = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - F(\theta) + g(r)\), where \(F' = f\) and \(g\) is a function of the radius.
  1. The third strain \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}\theta} = 0\) gives \(\frac1r f'(\theta) + \frac{4B\theta}{E} + g'(r) - \frac1r\big(\frac{4Br\theta}{E} - F(\theta) + g(r)\big) = 0\). The terms with \(\theta\) cancel. After multiplying by \(r\) what remains is \(f'(\theta) + F(\theta) = g(r) - r\,g'(r)\) at every point of the annulus. The left side is a function of \(\theta\) only and the right side of \(r\) only. On the radius at the angle \(\theta_1\) the left side is \(f'(\theta_1) + F(\theta_1)\) everywhere, so the right side has the same value for all \(r\), say \(c\). On the circle of radius \(r_2\) the right side is \(c\) everywhere, so the left side also equals \(c\) for all \(\theta\). The radius and the circle meet at the point \(T\). Both sides are therefore constant, \(= c\). From \(g - r\,g' = c\) it follows that \((g/r)' = (r g' - g)/r^2 = -c/r^2\), so \(g/r = c/r + W\) and \(g = c + W\,r\). The function \(F\) has the second derivative \(F'' = f'\) and \(F'' + F = c\), so \(G = F - c\) satisfies \(G'' + G = 0\). The functions \(W_1 = G'\cos\theta + G\sin\theta\) and \(W_2 = G\cos\theta - G'\sin\theta\) have, by theorem 8.13, the derivatives \(W_1' = (G'' + G)\cos\theta = 0\) and \(W_2' = -(G'' + G)\sin\theta = 0\), so they are constant (corollary 1.86), say \(W_1 = Q\) and \(W_2 = -P\). From \(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta = 1\) we get \(G = W_1\sin\theta + W_2\cos\theta = Q\sin\theta - P\cos\theta\). Then \(f = F' = Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta\) and \(u_\theta = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - F + g = 4B\,r\,\theta/E - Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta - c + c + W\,r\). This is (11.83). The field \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = Q\cos\theta + P\sin\theta\), \(u_\theta = -Q\sin\theta + P\cos\theta\) is the displacement \((Q, P)\) in local components, and \(u_\theta = W\,r\) is a rotation about \(O\) by \(W\).

3. Uniqueness.

  1. The displacement of the whole annulus is a function of the point, so at the point with the same \(r\) and \(\theta\) and at \(\theta + 2\pi\) it has the same value. The local components \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\), \(u_\theta\) then also return after going around, because \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) are functions of the point. Figure 11.158 draws \(u_\theta\) at a fixed \(r\) over the axis \(\theta\) from \(0\) to \(2\pi\). All terms of (11.83) except \(4B\,r\,\theta/E\) are periodic in \(\theta\) with period \(2\pi\), so their sum returns to its starting height at \(2\pi\). The term \(4B\,r\,\theta/E\), however, grows in proportion to \(\theta\), so from the start to the end of the turn \(u_\theta\) grows by \(8\pi B\,r/E\), which for \(r > 0\) differs from zero if \(B \ne 0\). So for \(B \ne 0\) there is no displacement field on the whole annulus. The jump \(8\pi B\,r/E\) grows in proportion to \(r\), like the width of the wedge \(\alpha r\) in figure 11.162 on the left. Such a displacement belongs to a ring that we open or close at a cut by the angle \(8\pi B/E\), at \(B = 49\) MPa and \(E = 196\) GPa by \(0{,}006283\), which is \(0{,}36^\circ\) (example 11.56). A whole annulus has no cut, so only \(B = 0\) remains for it.
  2. For \(B = 0\) the stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + 2C\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -A/r^2 + 2C\), so the form \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A_{\mathrm{L}} - B_{\mathrm{L}}/r^2\), \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = A_{\mathrm{L}} + B_{\mathrm{L}}/r^2\) of theorem 11.28 with \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 2C\) and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = -A\). At \(B = 0\) we have \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac1E\big[-(1+\nu)A/r + 2(1-\nu)C\,r\big] + \dots\), which is \(u_{\mathrm{r}} = \frac{(1-\nu)A_{\mathrm{L}}}{E}\,r + \frac{(1+\nu)B_{\mathrm{L}}}{E}\,\frac1r\), the displacement of theorem 11.28 at \(S = 0\), and \(u_\theta = W r + P\cos\theta - Q\sin\theta\) is a rigid motion.

Source: SADD (8.3.7)-(8.3.9) (PDF p. 187-188, crops (8.3.7), (8.3.8), (8.3.9) read). SADD calls the constants of the function \(\varphi\) \(a_1\), \(a_2\), \(a_3\) (here \(A\), \(C\), \(B\)) and the constants of the rigid motion \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) (here \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\)), but because the letters \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) are already taken here, we renamed them. On p. 188 SADD says that the term with \(a_3\) in \(u_\theta\) leads to multivalued displacements if a closed curve can be drawn around the origin inside the body. BARBER (PDF p. 132) says the same for the terms \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\). The integration with the functions \(f\) and \(g\) and the solution for \(F\) are ours, and SymPy checked that \(u_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(u_\theta\) of (11.83) satisfy all three strain equations identically.

The theorem showed three things. The three constants \(A\), \(B\), \(C\) give an axisymmetric stress field that satisfies equilibrium and the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\). Displacements are obtained only by integrating the strains, because the stresses alone do not say whether the ring has a displacement field without a jump across the cut. So single-valuedness of the displacement is a separate condition, as we already saw for the ring in chapter 4 (corollary 4.114, lemma 4.121): the compatibility equations are not enough for a body with a hole. And in a whole ring this condition removes the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\), while in a ring with a cut it leaves it.

From history

Michell investigated two-dimensional problems in a paper on the direct determination of stress in an elastic solid (On the direct determination of stress in an elastic solid), published in the Proceedings of the London Mathematical Society (BARBER, PDF p. 132, TIMO, PDF p. 292). BARBER attributes to him the general solution with stresses in the form of a Fourier series in \(\theta\) (definition 9.110) and calls it the Michell solution (BARBER, PDF p. 132). SADD says that Michell originally developed this solution in 1899 and that he restricts it to solutions periodic in \(\theta\), because then arbitrary boundary conditions can be treated with the Fourier method (SADD, PDF p. 187). LOVE, in the appendix on Volterra's theory of dislocations, says that Michell explicitly treated the possibility that the stress function is many-valued if the displacements are single-valued, and gives the year 1900 (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The years do not agree: 1899 (TIMO, BARBER, SADD) or 1900 (LOVE). Which year is right we cannot decide from these sources. LOVE justifies single-valued displacements like this: an actual displacement appears to be necessarily single-valued, but in a body that surrounds a hole, for example in a hollow cylinder, a many-valued displacement is also physically possible. From the cylinder we remove a thin slice between two axial planes, and the new surfaces are pressed together and joined. The body formed in this way is in an initial stress, which we obtain if the ratio of the displacement, resolved at right angles to the axial plane through the point, to the distance from the axis is many-valued with a cyclic constant, and we adjust the constant so that the corresponding points of the two axial planes coincide after the displacement (LOVE, PDF p. 240). The possibility of such an interpretation was, according to LOVE, first indicated by Weingarten in 1901, Timpe treated it in more detail for two-dimensional systems, among them the plane circular ring, and Volterra developed a more general theory in a series of notes and presented it comprehensively in 1907. Volterra calls the kind of deformations to which the theory applies "distorsioni", and Love says he ventured to call them dislocations (dislocations) (LOVE, PDF p. 240).

We asked what the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) does in a ring. By the theorem it is absent in a whole ring, and the history tells how a many-valued displacement was given a physical meaning: a body from which a wedge is cut out and which is joined again. Let us now compute such rings, first a ring in which \(B = 0\).

Example 11.55 The tube from the Airy function (cev iz Airyjeve funkcije)

The tube of section 11.7 has inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, pressure \(p = 30\) MPa in the bore, a free outer surface and free ends. This time we do not guess the displacements. We take \(\varphi = A\ln r + C\,r^2\), so \(B = 0\), because the tube surrounds a hole (theorem 11.54, item 3).

  1. On the circle \(r = a\) the outer normal of the body is \(\vek n = -\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\). The force per unit area there is \(-p\,\vek n = p\,\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and must equal \(\ten\sigma\,\vek n = -\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\vek e_{\mathrm{r}} - \sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}\vek e_\theta\), so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = -p\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(a) = 0\). At \(r = b\) we have \(\vek n = \vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and the force is zero, so \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{r}\theta}(b) = 0\). The shear stress is zero everywhere by the theorem, two equations remain by the expression (11.82), two points of a line above the axis \(1/r^2\):
    \[\frac{A}{a^2} + 2C = -p , \qquad \frac{A}{b^2} + 2C = 0 .\]
  2. The difference of the equations is \(A\,(1/a^2 - 1/b^2) = -p\). This is the slope of the line: the change of the stress by \(-p\) over the change of the number \(1/r^2\) by \(1/a^2 - 1/b^2\). So \(A = -p\,a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2) = -30 \cdot 1600 \cdot 3600/2000 = -86\,400\) MPa mm\(^2\). From the second equation \(2C = -A/b^2 = 86\,400/3600 = 24\) MPa, which is the value of the line at \(1/r^2 = 0\), so \(C = 12\) MPa.
  3. The stresses are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = 24 - 86\,400/r^2\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 24 + 86\,400/r^2\) in MPa with \(r\) in mm. At \(r = 40\), \(50\), \(60\) mm we have \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -30\), \(-10{,}56\), \(0\) MPa and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = 78\), \(58{,}56\), \(48\) MPa. The values \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = -30\) and \(0\) MPa are the slopes of the tangents at \(r = 40\) and \(60\) mm in figure 11.143, right, divided by \(r\). These are the same results as in theorem 11.28 with \(A_{\mathrm{L}} = 24\) MPa and \(B_{\mathrm{L}} = 86\,400\) MPa mm\(^2\).
  4. Because \(B = 0\), the displacements of item 3 of theorem 11.54 are Lamé's and single-valued, with no jump like the one at the cut. Because \(\sigma_{\mathrm{zz}} = 0\) at the free ends of the tube, the stresses are the same as in theorem 11.28 at \(S = 0\). There the field is shown to be an exact three-dimensional solution of the boundary problem, and by theorem 11.4 the only one up to a rigid motion.

Without the condition of single-valuedness the two boundary conditions do not determine the solution. For \(B \neq 0\) the same two conditions \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = -p\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\) would give different \(A\) and \(C\) for every \(B\). For \(B = 10\) MPa (in the expressions we write \(\ln(r/a)\) instead of \(\ln r\), which changes only \(C\), because \(r^2\ln r = r^2\ln(r/a) + r^2\ln a\)) we get \(A = -63\,045\) MPa mm\(^2\).
