Figure 11.160 shows both fields over the axis \(r\). The radial stress differs from the one at \(B = 0\) by at most \(0{,}81\) MPa. The hoop stress is \(68{,}81\), \(59{,}08\), \(55{,}03\) MPa at \(r = 40\), \(50\), \(60\) mm, instead of \(78\), \(58{,}56\), \(48\) MPa at \(B = 0\). This field too is in equilibrium and satisfies the boundary conditions, but by item 3 of the theorem it has a many-valued displacement, so it is not the field of a tube loaded by pressure alone. The choice \(B = 0\) is determined by the single-valuedness of the displacement, not by a boundary condition.

The stresses of Lamé's tube do not contain \(E\) and \(\nu\). This agrees with Michell's condition from section 11.10.4: for a region with a hole the stresses are independent of the moduli if the resultant of the forces on each edge is zero. For the tube the resultant of the pressure on each of the two circles is zero by symmetry, and in that section we only stated the condition, we did not prove it.

For a loading with forces that gives an axisymmetric field, \(B = 0\) therefore always holds in a ring that surrounds a hole. But what if the ring is not loaded by forces and instead we prescribe a jump of the displacement across a cut, like the ring with shortened fibres in chapter 4?

Example 11.56 A ring with a wedge removed (obroč z izrezanim klinom)

Take the ring of chapter 4: a thin steel ring with inner radius \(a = 40\) mm, outer radius \(b = 60\) mm, thickness \(2\) mm, modulus \(E = 196\) GPa and \(\nu = 0{,}3\). There we shortened all the fibres around the hole by \(k = 0{,}001\) and computed that the sides of the cut move apart by \(2\pi k\,r\), that is, by \(0{,}251\) mm at \(r = 40\) mm and \(0{,}377\) mm at \(r = 60\) mm (lemma 4.121). Now we do the opposite (figure 11.162, left). From a ring without stress we cut out a wedge with the angle \(\alpha = 2\pi k = 0{,}006283\) (\(0{,}36^\circ\)) with its apex at \(O\). The two sides of the wedge lie on radii through \(O\), so the wedge is \(\alpha r\) wide, that is, \(0{,}251\) mm and \(0{,}377\) mm at the edges, like the gap in chapter 4. We press the sides of the cut together and weld them. What stresses remain in a ring that no external force loads? The ring is thin and lies freely in the plane, so we take plane stress.

  1. We treat the ring with \(\varphi = A\ln(r/a) + B\,r^2\ln(r/a) + C'\,r^2\) by item 1 of lemma 11.51 (replacing \(\ln r\) by \(\ln(r/a) = \ln r - \ln a\) adds the term \(-B\ln a\,r^2\), which \(C'\) takes up, and the constant \(-A\ln a\), which gives no stress). The stresses by theorem 11.54 are \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} = A/r^2 + B\,(1 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C'\) and \(\sigma_{\theta\theta} = -A/r^2 + B\,(3 + 2\ln(r/a)) + 2C'\).
  1. Before welding the ring occupies the angles \(\alpha/2 \le \theta \le 2\pi - \alpha/2\), and between the extensions of the sides through \(O\) lies the angle \(\alpha\) (enlarged in figure 11.161). The point \(P^+\) on the radius \(r\) at \(\theta = \alpha/2\) and the point \(P^-\) on the same radius at \(\theta = 2\pi - \alpha/2\), one on each of the sides of the cut, are apart by \(2r\sin(\alpha/2) \approx \alpha r\) in the direction \(\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\), in which \(\vek e_\theta\) points on both sides to first order in \(\alpha\). After welding they must be at the same point, \(P^+ + \vek u^+ = P^- + \vek u^-\), so \(\vek u^- - \vek u^+ = \alpha r\,\vek e_{\mathrm{y}}\) must hold, and in local components \(u_\theta(2\pi - \alpha/2) - u_\theta(\alpha/2) = \alpha r\) (the computation is first order in \(\alpha\): we neglect the deviations of the bases \(\vek e_{\mathrm{r}}\) and \(\vek e_\theta\) between the two sides, which are of order \(\alpha = 0{,}006\), and the products of displacements with them, so the relative error is of order \(\alpha\), that is below \(1\,\%\)). By expression (11.83) the left side is \(4B\,r\,(2\pi - \alpha)/E \approx 8\pi B\,r/E\), since the rigid motion with \(P\), \(Q\) and \(W\) moves both sides equally. So \(B = E\alpha/(8\pi) = E k/4 = 49\) MPa. The jump of the displacement is thus \(2\pi k\,r\), as in chapter 4, only with the opposite sign: there the sides move apart, here we close them.
  2. The remaining constants are computed from the free surfaces, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(a) = 0\) and \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}(b) = 0\):
    \[\frac{A}{a^2} + B + 2C' = 0 , \qquad \frac{A}{b^2} + B\,\big(1 + 2\ln\tfrac ba\big) + 2C' = 0 .\]
    The difference is \(A\,(1/a^2 - 1/b^2) = 2B\ln(b/a)\), so \(A = 2B\ln(b/a)\,a^2 b^2/(b^2 - a^2) = 114\,438\) MPa mm\(^2\), and \(2C' = -A/a^2 - B = -71{,}52 - 49 = -120{,}52\) MPa. The stresses in MPa at \(r\) in mm are in the table, and figure 11.162, right, shows both as curves, with the radius \(r\) on the horizontal axis and the stress on the vertical one:
\(r\) [mm] 40 45 50 55 60
\(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\) \(0\) \(-3{,}47\) \(-3{,}88\) \(-2{,}48\) \(0\)
\(\sigma_{\theta\theta}\) \(-45{,}05\) \(-18{,}49\) \(2{,}57\) \(19{,}85\) \(34{,}42\)

The hoop stress is compressive at the inner edge, \(-45{,}05\) MPa, and tensile at the outer one, \(34{,}42\) MPa, and is zero at \(r = 49{,}33\) mm. The radial stress is compressive everywhere and at most \(3{,}99\) MPa in absolute value at \(r = 48{,}3\) mm. With \(B = 0\), that is without the wedge, the equations of step 3 would give \(A = 0\) and \(C' = 0\), and all stresses would be zero. So all these stresses come from the wedge. The field at \(B = 10\) MPa of example 11.55 is therefore the pressurized tube with a welded wedge added: the difference of the two tube fields has free faces and \(B = 10\) MPa, so it is this field multiplied by \(10/49\). That is why the hoop stresses in figure 11.160 cross at the same \(r = 49{,}33\) mm.

  1. The resultant of the hoop stresses on a cross section is zero. From the first equation of equilibrium in cylindrical axes, \(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}' + (\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} - \sigma_{\theta\theta})/r = 0\), we get \((r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}})' = \sigma_{\theta\theta}\), so \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,\mathrm{d}r = \big[r\,\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}}\big]_{\mathrm{a}}^b = 0\) by the free surfaces. In figure 11.162, right, the area below the axis and the area above it, both between the blackwhite curve and the axis \(r\), are therefore equal. The moment of the hoop stresses about \(O\) is not zero: \(\int_{\mathrm{a}}^b\sigma_{\theta\theta}\,r\,\mathrm{d}r = 2599\) N mm per millimetre of thickness, for the thickness \(2\) mm it is \(5{,}198\) N m. Every cross section thus carries a moment without a force, compression at the inner and tension at the outer edge. We will meet the same form of \(\varphi\) in section 11.14, in a beam in the shape of an arc, where the moment is prescribed at the ends of the beam and the cut stays open.

The stresses are proportional to \(E\), because \(B = E\alpha/(8\pi)\) and \(A\) and \(C'\) are proportional to \(B\). They do not contain \(\nu\), because \(\nu\) appears neither in \(B\) nor in the equations for \(A\) and \(C'\): the datum is a jump of displacement, not a force. This is not in contradiction with Michell's independence of the moduli, which holds for a loading with forces with zero resultant on each edge. The term \(4B/E\) in \(\frac1r\,\partial u_\theta/\partial\theta\) equals \(\alpha/(2\pi) = k\), that is, the relative shortening of the circumference by the wedge, \(\alpha r/(2\pi r)\). Because \(\varepsilon_{\mathrm{zz}} = -\nu(\sigma_{\mathrm{rr}} + \sigma_{\theta\theta})/E\) here depends on \(r\) (from \(6{,}9\cdot10^{-5}\) at \(r = 40\) mm to \(-5{,}3\cdot10^{-5}\) at \(60\) mm), the model of plane stress does not satisfy all the compatibility equations in three dimensions (theorem 11.37), so the field holds as an average over the thickness of the thin ring (theorem 11.39).

The section gave the polar form of the Airy stresses (lemma 11.50), the powers and the logarithm that solve the equation \(\nabla^4\varphi = 0\) (lemma 11.51), and the axisymmetric case with the single-valuedness that removes the term \(B\,r^2\ln r\) in a whole ring (theorem 11.54). With it we computed the tube once more, this time from the stresses, and computed a ring with a wedge removed, in which the same term describes stresses without an external force. We saved the terms with \(n = 1\) and \(n = 2\) of lemma 11.51: with \(n = 2\) we will solve in section 11.13 the plane problem with a round hole, and with \(n = 0\) and \(n = 1\) in section 11.14 a beam in the shape of an arc.
